There could be extenuating circumstances about this incident that I don't know, but as much as I dislike Facebook and want to see them suffer, I think it sets a bad precedent to punish companies for bugs in software like this. EVERY PIECE OF SOFTWARE longer than a few lines of code has errors that theoretically allow attackers to break into it. This kind of law could be used to put complete risk and uncertainty into the software industry, and be used by evil bureaucrats to punish their enemies. Troubling precedent.

And what more could Facebook reasonably do? Consider that they have many teams of people that already do code reviews and massive security teams to check sites for errors and already do as much as humanly possible to ensure that only they have access to user data and they still got breached.

Also, this note from the article is troubling "the GDPR contains recommendations that companies store as little user data as necessary, potentially exposing Facebook to higher liability". As much as Facebook is anti-privacy and bad for your mental-health, who is some government bureaucrat to decide how much data is necessary or not? All of these have troubling implications for the future of innovation. Not saying I support Facebook at all, but individuals should be making decisions and not old government bureaucrats who barely understand these issues or what consequences their mandates might lead to.
